text.title: How Plants Disperse Their Seeds
text.body:
Because plants cannot move, they depend on other means to carry their seeds away from the parent. Dispersal matters: a seedling that sprouts directly beneath its parent must compete with it for light, water and nutrients, and is often more vulnerable to pests that have built up nearby.

Many species rely on wind. Dandelion seeds hang beneath tiny parachutes of fine hairs, while maple seeds have wings that make them spin slowly to the ground, giving the breeze more time to carry them. Animals are another common carrier. Some plants surround their seeds with sweet fruit; birds swallow the fruit and later deposit the seeds, often far away. Others, such as burdock, produce hooked burrs that cling to fur.

Plants near rivers and coasts may use water instead. The coconut, for example, has a fibrous husk that allows it to float across oceans for many weeks. A few plants need no carrier at all. As the pods of certain species dry out, tension builds in their walls until they suddenly burst, flinging seeds several metres away.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why is it a disadvantage for a seedling to grow directly beneath its parent?
options: It is usually eaten by the animals that carry seeds.
It has to compete with its parent for resources.
It sprouts later than seedlings carried by wind.
It is too heavy to be moved by water or wind.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says such a seedling 'must compete with it for light, water and nutrients'.

questions.prompt: The word "deposit" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: leave
swallow
collect
hide
questions.explanation: Birds swallow the fruit and later 'deposit' (leave) the seeds somewhere else.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention maple seeds?
options: To contrast seeds carried by wind with seeds carried by water
To show that some seeds are too heavy for the wind
To explain why some trees produce sweet fruit
To give an example of a seed shaped to stay in the air longer
questions.explanation: Maple seeds have wings that make them spin slowly, 'giving the breeze more time to carry them'.

options: Floating across water

questions.explanation: Water, burrs on fur and bursting pods are all described, but insects burying seeds are never mentioned.

options: Drying out triggers the release of their seeds.
They grow mainly along rivers and coasts.
They depend on birds to open their pods.
Their seeds travel farther than coconuts.
questions.explanation: Tension builds 'as the pods of certain species dry out' until they burst, so drying is what releases the seeds.

text.title: How Octopuses Change Colour
text.body:
Octopuses can change the colour of their skin in less than a second. They do this with thousands of special cells called chromatophores. Each chromatophore is a small bag of colour, such as red, yellow or brown, with tiny muscles around it. When the muscles pull, the bag gets wider and the colour becomes easy to see. When the muscles relax, the bag gets smaller and the colour almost disappears.

The main reason octopuses change colour is to hide. By matching the colours of rocks, sand or plants around them, they become very hard for hungry fish to see. This kind of hiding is called camouflage. Some octopuses can even change the texture of their skin so that it looks bumpy like a rock.

Colour is also used to send messages. An octopus may turn dark or flash quickly to frighten an enemy, or show certain colours to another octopus. Scientists are still studying exactly what these signals mean.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says each chromatophore 'is a small bag of colour' with tiny muscles around it.

options: The colour becomes brighter.
The bag gets wider.

The skin becomes bumpy.
questions.explanation: 'When the muscles relax, the bag gets smaller and the colour almost disappears.'

questions.explanation: An octopus turns dark or flashes to 'frighten' (scare) an enemy away.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 opens with 'The main reason octopuses change colour is to hide' and describes camouflage.

text.title: Library Services: Changes to Student Printing Allowances
text.body:
From the start of the spring term, the annual printing allowance for undergraduates will be replaced by a termly allowance of 300 black-and-white pages (each colour page counts as four). Unused allowance pages will no longer roll over between terms, a change prompted by the large number of credits that went unspent each summer. Students who exhaust their allowance may top up through the student portal in blocks of 50 pages; top-ups remain valid until they are used, regardless of when they were bought.

Postgraduate research students are exempt and should continue to request printing through their department. Undergraduates whose course requires extensive printing, for example architecture portfolios, may apply for an additional free allowance, provided the application is supported by a course leader. Applications submitted after week 3 will be considered only in exceptional circumstances.

text.title: Railways and the Creation of Standard Time
text.body:
Until the mid-nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, setting their clocks by the position of the sun. Because noon arrives slightly later as one travels west, a town's clocks could differ by several minutes from those of a neighbouring town. For communities whose contact with one another was limited by the speed of a horse, such discrepancies were of little consequence.

The railways changed this. A train could cover in hours a distance that once took days, and timetables that listed dozens of local times became both confusing and dangerous, since trains sharing a single track depended on precise scheduling to avoid collisions. In 1847, many British railway companies adopted Greenwich Mean Time, and towns gradually followed, although it was not made the legal time for Britain until 1880.

North America faced a far larger problem, as its railways spanned several thousand kilometres. In 1883, the railroads of the United States and Canada introduced a system of standard time zones, and the following year an international conference in Washington chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, laying the foundation for the global time zones still used today.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "the speed of a horse" in paragraph 1?
options: To show that horses were once faster than early trains
To suggest that riders carried the correct time between towns
To explain why differences in local time once caused few problems
To argue that local time was more accurate than railway time
questions.explanation: Because travel was limited to horse speed, the small differences between towns 'were of little consequence'.

questions.prompt: The word "discrepancies" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: agreements
differences
delays
measurements
questions.explanation: 'Such discrepancies' refers back to clocks that 'could differ by several minutes', so it means differences.

options: Trains sharing a track needed exact timing to avoid crashes.
Passengers often missed trains and walked along the tracks.
Station clocks were reset by the sun every morning.
Drivers could not read timetables with so many columns.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says trains 'sharing a single track depended on precise scheduling to avoid collisions'.

options: It was used by railways but rejected by every town.
It was required by law in all British towns.
It was abandoned by most railway companies.
It was widely used before it became the legal time.
questions.explanation: Railways adopted it in 1847 and towns 'gradually followed', although it only became legal time in 1880.

questions.explanation: The railroads introduced time zones in 1883; the Washington conference came the following year and chose the prime meridian.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an ornithology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: OK, so if you've ever camped in spring, you'll know that birds are loudest just before and around sunrise. Ornithologists call this the dawn chorus. And the obvious question is, why then? Why not at noon? Well, there are a few explanations, and they aren't mutually exclusive. The first is about sound. In the early morning the air's usually still and cool, with less wind, so a song carries further. A male defending his territory gets more distance for the same effort. The second is about food. At first light it's too dark to spot insects easily, and many insects aren't active yet in the cold. So rather than forage badly, a bird might as well sing. The third explanation is my favourite. A small bird can lose a surprising share of its body weight overnight just keeping warm. So a male that sings loudly at dawn is basically announcing: I made it through the night, and I've still got energy to spare. To a female, or to a rival, that's an honest signal of good condition. Now, researchers still argue about which factor matters most, and it probably varies from species to species. But together, they go a long way toward explaining why dawn is prime time.

questions.explanation: Because the night is costly, a loud dawn song shows the male still has 'energy to spare', an honest signal of good condition.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a history of cartography class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's start with a problem every mapmaker faces. The Earth's surface is curved, and you simply can't flatten a curved surface without stretching or tearing it. Try flattening an orange peel on a table and you'll see what I mean. So every flat map distorts something: shape, area, distance or direction. The real question is what you choose to keep. In 1569, Gerardus Mercator chose direction. On his projection, a line of constant compass bearing is a straight line. For sailors that was enormously useful. Draw a line from port to port, measure the angle, and follow your compass. But there's a price. To keep the angles correct, Mercator had to stretch the map more and more toward the poles. That's why Greenland looks roughly the size of Africa, even though Africa is about fourteen times larger.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: So why do online maps still use it?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Good question. Because it keeps local shapes accurate. When you zoom in on a street corner, a right angle looks like a right angle. That matters far more to someone looking for a café than the size of Greenland does. So Mercator isn't wrong, exactly. It's a tool designed for a particular job.

How sailors used compasses before maps existed

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a food science class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today we're looking at something you've all seen in your kitchen: stale bread. Most people think bread goes stale because it dries out. But that's not really the main reason. The real cause is starch. Flour is mostly starch. When bread bakes, the starch soaks up water and becomes soft. Then, as the bread cools and sits, the starch molecules slowly line up again into hard, tight structures. Scientists call this retrogradation. Water gets pushed out of the starch, and the bread feels firm and dry, even if very little water has left the loaf. Here's a simple test. Put a slice in a sealed plastic bag. It can't dry out, but after a few days it's still stale. So what can you do? Well, don't keep bread in the fridge. Cold temperatures just above freezing actually make staling faster. The freezer is much better, because it stops the process. And if your bread is already a bit stale, warm it in the oven or the toaster. The heat softens the starch again, at least for a while.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How to bake bread at home
Why bread becomes stale
Why flour contains water
How fridges keep food fresh
questions.explanation: The professor introduces 'stale bread' and explains that starch, not drying, is the main cause.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, where does bread go stale faster?
options: In the freezer
In a paper bag
In the oven
In the fridge
questions.explanation: She says not to keep bread in the fridge because cold temperatures 'make staling faster'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention a slice of bread in a sealed plastic bag?
options: To show that bread goes stale even when it can't dry out
To explain the best way to store bread
To show how much water bread contains
To compare plastic bags with paper bags
questions.explanation: The sealed slice 'can't dry out, but after a few days it's still stale', so drying is not the main cause.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about warming stale bread?
options: It keeps the bread fresh for weeks.
It removes the starch from the bread.
The bread will become stale again later.
It only works in a toaster.
questions.explanation: The heat softens the starch only 'for a while', so the bread will go stale again.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a materials engineering class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Concrete is the most widely used building material on Earth, and it has one persistent weakness: it cracks. Now, small cracks aren't dangerous in themselves. The trouble is what gets in through them. Water seeps down to the steel reinforcing bars, the steel rusts, and rust takes up more space than the original metal, so it pushes the concrete apart from the inside. Repairing that by hand is costly, and on a bridge or in a tunnel it's often impractical. So here's an elegant workaround developed by researchers in the Netherlands. You mix bacterial spores into the concrete, along with a food source, calcium lactate. The bacteria are chosen because they can survive concrete's extreme alkalinity, which would kill most microbes. The spores lie dormant, potentially for decades. When a crack forms and water gets in, they wake up, feed on the lactate, and produce calcium carbonate, essentially limestone, which plugs the crack. It's a bit like a cut that scabs over. Now, I don't want to oversell this. It works on hairline cracks, under a millimetre or so, not on major structural failures. And it's considerably more expensive than ordinary concrete, so for now it makes most sense where repairs would be hardest to carry out.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why concrete is stronger than steel
A method that lets concrete seal its own small cracks
How bacteria cause concrete to crack
The history of bridge and tunnel building
questions.explanation: After explaining why cracks matter, the professor describes bacteria that 'plug the crack' inside concrete.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why are cracks in concrete a problem?
options: They let water reach the steel, which rusts and expands.
They make buildings look older than they are.
They allow harmful bacteria to escape.
They immediately reduce the weight the concrete can carry.
questions.explanation: Water reaches the steel bars, and rust 'takes up more space' and pushes the concrete apart.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor compare the process to a cut that scabs over?
options: To show that the bacteria can be harmful to people
To explain why the repair takes several weeks
To argue that concrete is a living material
To give a familiar image of a material sealing its own damage
questions.explanation: The everyday image of a scab helps listeners picture the crack being sealed from within.

options: He expects it to replace ordinary concrete soon.

He thinks it is too risky to use in bridges.
questions.explanation: He calls it 'elegant' but says 'I don't want to oversell this' and lists its limits on crack size and cost.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a business class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: In business there's a widespread belief that being first to market is a huge advantage. And sometimes it is. A first mover can build brand recognition before anyone else, secure patents, and lock in the best suppliers or locations. And if customers face switching costs, say, they've learned your software or stored all their data with you, they may never leave. But the evidence is, well, more mixed than the slogan suggests. First movers carry the cost of educating the market. They have to convince people they need a product that didn't exist before. And they make the early mistakes. A fast follower can watch, learn what customers actually want, and enter with a better version at a lower development cost. Search engines are a classic case. By the time Google launched in 1998, AltaVista and Lycos were already well known.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: So being first is actually a disadvantage?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Not quite. I'd say timing on its own is overrated as a strategy. What matters is whether you can hold the lead. If network effects or patents protect you, being first is great. If not, you've just done your competitors' research for them.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How Google became the largest search engine
Why patents are expensive for new companies
Why companies should always enter a market first
Whether being first to market is really an advantage
questions.explanation: The professor questions the 'widespread belief' that being first is a huge advantage and weighs both sides.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what is one advantage of being a fast follower?
options: Owning the earliest patents
Benefiting from customers' switching costs
Learning from the first mover's mistakes
Building brand recognition before rivals
questions.explanation: A fast follower 'can watch, learn what customers actually want' after the first mover makes 'the early mistakes'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention AltaVista and Lycos?
options: To show that a later entrant can overtake established pioneers
To identify the very first search engine
To explain how network effects work
To argue that search engines need strong patents
questions.explanation: They were already well known when Google launched, illustrating a fast follower succeeding.

questions.prompt: What does the professor mean when she says "you've just done your competitors' research for them"?
options: First movers should share their research openly.
Without protection, a first mover's efforts mainly help rivals.
Competitors usually pay for market research.
Research is the largest cost in most businesses.
questions.explanation: If nothing protects the lead, rivals simply learn from the first mover's costly work and benefit from it.

items.prompt: The career fair is in the main hall on Thursday.

items.prompt: Why is the lecture hall locked this afternoon?

items.prompt: Who is the woman at the front desk?

items.prompt: Why did you go back to your dorm before class?

items.prompt: Have you submitted the scholarship application form?
items.explanation: Not yet, I still need to fill it out by Friday: 'still' goes before the main verb, and a pronoun object goes between the verb and particle ('fill it out').

items.prompt: What did your supervisor ask in the meeting?
items.explanation: She wanted to know whether we had enough time to finish the report: reported yes/no question with 'whether' and statement word order.

items.prompt: Did you apply for the summer internship at the bank?
items.explanation: No, but I would have applied if I had known about it earlier: third conditional (would have + past participle, if + past perfect).
Not only did she finish early, but she also answered every question: after 'not only' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject (did she).
